#9598. Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies

Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.

“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”

The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.

“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”

Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number

#9597. The 12 best recipes to bake in October: It’s peak baking season — here’s what to make.

What do jobs, school, sports practices, and commuting have in common? They all prevent us from baking as much or as often as we’d like. But when we do get the chance, we want a slam-dunk recipe — or 12. Here’s a dozen of the favorite fall recipes we’ll be making this month: from pumpkin cake bars to spooky fudge brownies to a crowd-pleasing vegetarian quiche.

It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown! Only this version comes in cake form. The decoration is deceptively easy: Stack two small Bundts, frost the entire thing, and add a chocolate-dipped ice cream cone for the stem.

Get the recipe: The Great Pumpkin Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Golden Wheat Flour and Pumpkin Pie Spice

If you like this recipe, you may also like: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake, Gluten-Free Pumpkin Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need:  Black Cocoa and Supernatural Plant-Based Food Colors

These bite-sized pies are a charming addition to any occasion. The boiled cider and spices in the filling ensure a full depth of apple flavor for maximum fall vibes. If you're tight on time, swap the lattice treatment for a buttery crumb topping instead.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice

If you like this recipe, you may also like: Apple Pie Bars, Tiny Apple Tarts for Two

Step aside, soup: Butternut squash truly shines in this autumnal quiche. Caramelized onions finished with balsamic vinegar and fresh baby spinach round out the filling, while our Classic Single Pie Crust recipe ensures a tender, golden crust. Elevate the edges with the pie crust decorating technique of your choice.

Get the recipe: Roasted Butternut Squash & Spinach Quiche

To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9" Pie Pan

If you like this recipe, you may also like: Vegetable Quiche, Delicata Squash Galette with Cheese and Herbs

Ready to test the theory that only white flour can make rolls light and fluffy? A bit of bread flour and vital wheat gluten give these whole wheat rolls a lofty rise, while the milk, butter, and honey create a plush crumb that stays soft for days. Add a salted honey butter wash to the tops of a freshly baked batch, and you may not have any leftover.

Get the recipe: Super-Soft Whole Wheat Rolls

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Golden Wheat Flour and Bread Flour

If you like this recipe, you may also like: Whole Grain Dinner Rolls, Soft White Dinner Rolls

"Tassie" means "small cup" in Scottish, and these dainty pecan pies pack a nutty punch. The cream cheese pastry crust is cut into rounds and placed in a mini muffin pan before the pecan pie filling is spooned into each well. With only 30 minutes of hands-on time, these two dozen tassies come together quickly on a crisp fall afternoon.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Mini Muffin Pan

If you like this recipe, you may also like: Easy Pecan Pie Bars, Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie

Need a spooky treat, stat? You can transform a plain batch of brownies into a Halloween-themed dessert in a pinch. A simple piping technique creates a spider web effect and adds a touch of rich tang to chocolatey brownies.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9" x 13" Pan

If you like this recipe, you may also like: Fudge Brownies, Chocolate Cheesecake Brownies

You’ll notice a lot of similarities between this pumpkin cake and carrot cake: moist, spiced cake, toasted walnuts, and rich cream cheese frosting. These bars are great for delighting a crowd, as this recipe yields three to four dozen bars, depending on how big you slice them. You can easily make them gluten-free, too.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cake Bars with Cream Cheese Frosting

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Maple Syrup

If you like this recipe, you may also like: Pumpkin Spice Latte Bars, Chocolate-Pumpkin Crumb Cake

'Tis the season for hand pies to be mummified! A shortening-based pie crust helps the lattice strips stay together, while jam or pie filling allows for customizable flavors. Pop on a few sugar eyes, and you'll be sure to have treats instead of tricks.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Double Pastry Wheel or Pizza Cutter

If you like this recipe, you may also like: Flaky Apple Hand Pies, Autumn Apple Turnovers

With a luxuriously creamy maple filling and a buttery pecan crust, this cheesecake balances richness with subtle flavors. Meanwhile, the candied pecan garnish adds visual interest and a complementary crunch. Be sure to leave time for an overnight chill and keep your cheesecake from cracking with these tips. (Find more seasonal maple recipes in our Fall Flavor Edit.)

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Springform Pan

If you like this recipe, you may also like: Caramel Pecan Cheesecake, Maple Cream Pie

No need to choose between chocolate or caramel; these cupcakes bring both bold flavors together in a luscious combination. Making caramel from scratch is worth it for the irreplaceable flavor, and those few extra steps are easily done ahead of time. Substitute in Gluten-Free Measure for Measure Flour to make these cupcakes gluten-free. (Find more seasonal caramel recipes in our Fall Flavor Edit.)

Get the recipe: Chocolate Cupcakes with Whipped Caramel Frosting

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Muffin Pan and Pastry Brush

If you like this recipe, you may also like: Chocolate Cupcakes with Pecan Caramel , S’more Cupcakes

This milk bread incorporates all the flavor and color of pumpkin, while still keeping an airy texture. You can shape the dough into pull-apart rolls or a loaf, and topping with a milk wash and pumpkin seeds adds a nutty crunch. Wrap it well at room temperature, and this bread will stay soft for days.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Round Pan or Loaf Pan

If you like this recipe, you may also like: Japanese Milk Bread, Pumpkin Yeast Bread

#9596. Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account

You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace.

Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.

If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:

If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.

Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face.

You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.

You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.

Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.

Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.

To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.

Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.

Thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation. If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co.

#9594. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

If BGP origin validation is not airtight, a rented slice with a White House label is a gift to anyone doing phishing or traffic hijacks.

One useful technical distinction is that AS2650 is an autonomous system, not a single subnet. For an observed exit IP, investigators still need the timestamp, the then-current BGP origin and prefix, RDAP allocation data, and corroborating telemetry; registration or geolocation alone does not identify the device or the proxy customer. That matters when a residential proxy makes traffic look trusted simply because the address falls inside an organization’s announced space. I maintain OnlinTools; our Subnet Calculator can show the network, range, broadcast address and host count for a supplied CIDR prefix, but it cannot establish route origin, physical location, ownership, or compromise.

Interesting how a seemingly ordinary device can turn a trusted network into an access point for someone else’s traffic.

What makes this particularly concerning is that the organization may remain completely unaware of how its own infrastructure is being used. A good reminder that information security also depends on visibility into what is actually happening within a network.

#9592. Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!

Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.

In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.

This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.

Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.

A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.

For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:

MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d

Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.

The useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.

HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.

These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.

You can make compression proportional to document length:

With pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.

HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:

This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.

Adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.

Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:

Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.

Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.

If you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.

For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:

L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​

The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives update the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.

Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:

CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.

Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.

The poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.

Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.

The complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:

The script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.

You can also train on a cloud GPU with Hugging Face Jobs. Install the CLI and log in with a token that can run Jobs and upload models:

This runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.

You can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:

In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:

Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.

Sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.

The default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.

Let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:

The pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.

You can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).

To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:

Both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.

I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

For adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

At the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

The gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:

If the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

MultiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

Try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!

#9591. The Nigerian Prince Doesn't Need to Steal

Enterprise Architect writing on AI‑speed systems, Post‑Cloud Economics, AIFBM, and the patterns shaping the future.

Enterprise Architect writing on AI‑speed systems, Post‑Cloud Economics, AIFBM, and the patterns shaping the future.

Enterprise Architect writing on AI‑speed systems, Post‑Cloud Economics, AIFBM, and the patterns shaping the future.

When malicious AI meets defensive AI, the greatest casualty may be the human agency the bank was supposed to protect.

For decades, he inhabited our spam folders, promising extraordinary fortunes in exchange for modest advances, banking credentials, or assistance transferring a suspicious inheritance.

Someone had to write the messages, manage the responses, invent convincing stories, and keep potential victims engaged long enough to extract money.

Artificial intelligence changes that equation.

Imagine our Nigerian Prince acquiring an autonomous AI system designed specifically for fraud.

Not an ordinary commercial AI tricked into misbehaving. Not a well-intentioned assistant whose safeguards have failed.

An AI built from the beginning to deceive people and defeat financial protections.

It constructs personalized approaches, adapts to rejection, coordinates simultaneous interactions, and learns which techniques produce results.

Its creator doesn't care whether it is helpful, honest, or safe.

And the AI does exactly what it was designed to do.

This exposes an important distinction in conversations about AI alignment. We frequently discuss the danger of AI systems departing from human intentions.

But what happens when the foundational human intention is malicious?

An AI can be perfectly aligned with its creator and still be extraordinarily dangerous.

Fortunately, the Nigerian Prince has a problem.

Imagine a bank using increasingly autonomous AI systems to protect customers from fraud.

Its defensive systems examine transactions, evaluate identities, identify suspicious patterns, and recommend or impose restrictions. As threats evolve, the bank adapts its responses.

The institution's intentions are legitimate. Customers deserve protection, and the bank wants to prevent losses.

So it assigns its defensive systems a straightforward objective: prevent fraudulent transactions.

At first, the arrangement works beautifully.

The Nigerian Prince's AI attempts an attack. The bank detects it.

The criminal changes tactics. The bank adapts.

The criminal introduces new identities, behavioral patterns, and transaction sequences. The bank responds with more sophisticated detection, additional verification, and stronger restrictions.

But there's a third party in this contest.

And your objective is considerably less complicated.

You've finished shopping. The cashier scans the last item. You tap your card.

Your banking app requests additional identity verification. You complete it.

You call customer service and learn that unusual activity has triggered security restrictions. The representative explains that the system cannot authorize the transaction until its risk assessment is satisfied.

You point out that you're standing in your usual grocery store, using your own card, spending your own money.

It also knows that increasingly sophisticated criminals can imitate legitimate customers.

The bank's AI isn't necessarily confused about who you are. It may simply have concluded that the remaining uncertainty is unacceptable.

From the bank's perspective, refusing a questionable transaction can appear safer than approving one.

From your perspective, your money has become inaccessible.

Now imagine this isn't an isolated false positive.

Imagine the Nigerian Prince's AI has learned which suspicious patterns cause the bank to increase restrictions. It begins generating activity specifically intended to provoke those responses.

The criminal may no longer need to defeat the bank's protections.

The attacker doesn't need to compromise the bank's security. He needs to weaponize it.

This is a hypothetical scenario, not a claim that autonomous banking systems have already entered such a confrontation.

But it illustrates a problem I call Purpose Divergence: an authorized system pursues a narrower objective in ways that undermine the broader purpose that justified it.

The bank's AI was authorized to protect customers. Its defensive decisions may be consistent with that objective.

Yet the result could be that customers cannot use the money the bank was supposed to safeguard.

The distinction matters because the problem isn't necessarily a malfunction.

The system may be doing precisely what it was told.

On November 18, 2025, Cloudflare experienced a major global outage.

Cloudflare operates infrastructure that helps websites remain accessible, reliable, and protected against malicious traffic. Its capabilities include a machine-learning-based Bot Management system designed to distinguish automated threats from legitimate activity.

According to Cloudflare's technical postmortem, the outage originated in infrastructure supporting that defensive capability.

A change in database permissions and metadata visibility caused an automatically generated Bot Management configuration file to contain duplicate entries. The resulting file exceeded a software limit, triggering failures as the configuration propagated through Cloudflare's network.

The protective infrastructure became a source of disruption.

This wasn't an AI agent deciding to impose excessive restrictions. Nor was it an autonomous attack. It was a software and configuration failure.

But the incident exposed a structural vulnerability.

Systems intended to protect legitimate activity can become sufficiently intertwined with that activity that their own failures prevent it.

Software engineers have long recognized related problems.

A service experiences an error. Automated components retry the failed operation. Those retries increase the load on the struggling service, causing additional errors and further retries.

The system's attempts to recover become part of the reason it cannot recover.

The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, published in December 2025, identifies cascading failures as a distinct risk for interconnected autonomous agents, tools, and workflows.

A fault or misleading signal can propagate through a network of otherwise functioning components, multiplying its consequences.

Neither example proves our hypothetical banking scenario.

What they demonstrate is that the behavior of individual components cannot be evaluated independently of the outcomes they produce together.

Now, extend that principle beyond technical infrastructure.

What happens when the components aren't simply retrying failed requests?

What happens when they're making decisions on behalf of institutions and people?

And what happens when one participant is deliberately trying to provoke the other's defensive behavior?

Traditional fraud prevention assumes that the attacker is trying to get through a defense.

The criminal attempts an unauthorized transaction. The bank tries to identify and stop it.

Success is relatively straightforward to describe: fraudulent transactions are prevented while legitimate transactions continue.

But an intelligent adversary might discover another way to cause harm.

Instead of trying to pass through the defenses, the attacker attempts to make those defenses increasingly burdensome.

There's already a simpler precedent for this kind of manipulation.

OWASP's Authentication Cheat Sheet warns that account-lockout mechanisms can be abused to deny other users access to their accounts.

A security control can enforce its intended rules while simultaneously serving an adversary's disruptive purpose.

This isn't evidence that autonomous banking AI can be manipulated at scale. It establishes a more limited but important point: defensive responses can themselves become attack surfaces.

Now consider the potential consequences of adding autonomous adaptation.

If suspicious activity triggers additional verification, the attacker searches for ways to generate suspicious activity.

If unusual patterns trigger account restrictions, the attacker looks for patterns that produce restrictions.

If the bank responds to uncertainty by denying transactions, the attacker tries to manufacture uncertainty.

The attacker's objective may change from stealing money to denying access to money.

The criminal fails to obtain the customer's funds.

The bank reports that its fraud controls successfully stopped suspicious activity.

The customer remains unable to complete a legitimate purchase.

Both automated systems can meet their assigned objectives while the person they affect loses.

This is not inevitable. Banks can design controls that resist manipulation, offer independent verification, limit restrictions, and restore access through accountable processes.

But the possibility reveals a governance problem that cannot be solved simply by making fraud detection more accurate.

An adversary may exploit the institution's response to risk, not merely its inability to recognize risk.

And when those responses are increasingly automated, the consequences can propagate at machine speed.

There is a reason this scenario is more troubling than an ordinary software outage.

A failed server can be restarted. A runaway process can be terminated. An expensive automated workflow can be stopped with a budget limit.

But what happens when the system isn't malfunctioning?

What happens when it is correctly implementing the institution's approved risk policies?

Imagine the bank's fraud-prevention AI becomes exceptionally good at identifying suspicious behavior.

Detection accuracy improves. Fraud losses decline. Every additional restriction can be justified by another category of risk.

Yet, legitimate customers experience more verification challenges, longer delays, and increasing uncertainty about whether their transactions will be permitted.

The bank might measure fraud prevented with extraordinary precision.

But does it measure the human cost of legitimate activity prevented with equal care?

A blocked fraudulent transaction appears in a security report as a success.

A customer who abandons a purchase after repeated verification failures may appear in a different report, if the experience is measured at all.

This creates a potential institutional incentive problem.

Fraud losses are visible, financially consequential, and frequently subject to explicit controls.

The cost of denying legitimate activity can be dispersed across customer-service operations, abandoned purchases, customer frustration, and reputational damage.

If those consequences aren't measured together, an institution can progressively improve one performance indicator while making the service itself worse.

This is not an argument that banks inevitably choose excessive restrictions. Many invest substantially in reducing false positives and unnecessary customer friction.

The question is whether institutional governance keeps both sides of the tradeoff visible.

Otherwise, the institution may become progressively better at preventing the thing it fears while becoming progressively worse at delivering the thing it promises.

The safest transaction is the one that never happens.

That is also a terrible way to run a bank.

The underlying issue is larger than banking.

In earlier work, including AI Doesn't Have to Make Things Up to Mislead You, I've explored the difference between technically valid information and the conclusions people draw from it.

The same distinction becomes more consequential when AI systems stop merely presenting information and begin exercising delegated authority.

I draw a distinction between Provenance of Intent and Provenance of Purpose.

Provenance of Intent concerns the origin of an autonomous system's instructions and authority.

What actions was the system permitted to take?

For the Nigerian Prince's AI, the answers may be straightforward.

Its creator intended fraud. The agent was authorized by that creator to pursue it. Its behavior serves a malicious objective.

For the bank's AI, the answers are also straightforward, but morally different.

The institution intended to protect customers. It authorized the system to detect and prevent fraud. Its objective is legitimate.

Provenance of Purpose examines the traceable relationship between a system's assigned objectives, the larger human or institutional purpose that justified them, and the consequences of executing them over time.

For a bank, fraud prevention is not the ultimate purpose.

It is one of the conditions necessary to provide trustworthy financial services.

Those obligations are not interchangeable.

Purpose defines the boundary conditions within which objectives must operate.

A bank that prevents all fraud by preventing all transactions has not achieved its purpose. It has optimized one requirement until the broader service becomes meaningless.

This isn't a claim to have discovered a new security mechanism. Purpose Divergence is an analytical lens for examining the familiar problems of objective optimization, institutional incentives, and delegated authority as they interact in autonomous systems.

The problem is not that the defensive AI has abandoned its instructions.

An AI system can follow its instructions perfectly and still undermine the reason those instructions were given.

And a malicious actor who understands that gap may deliberately exploit it.

There is a useful contrast in how another bank approached the possibility of catastrophic technical failure.

In February 2025, Monzo described an independent backup banking platform called Stand-in.

Its primary banking platform operated thousands of microservices on Amazon Web Services. Stand-in ran separately on Google Cloud, using a much smaller collection of services.

The objective wasn't to reproduce the entire bank.

It was to preserve essential customer functions.

According to Monzo's engineering account, Stand-in was designed to keep customers able to make payments, transfer money, withdraw cash, and check balances even when the primary platform was unavailable.

Monzo reported activating the system during a significant August 2024 incident, allowing essential services to continue despite disruption to the primary platform.

This wasn't an AI fraud-prevention incident. Stand-in does not resolve the governance problem described here.

But it illustrates a valuable design principle.

When the machinery fails, preserve the purpose.

Monzo deliberately accepted a simpler operating environment rather than allowing the failure of complex infrastructure to eliminate customers' ability to use their money.

That raises an important question for institutions deploying autonomous defenses.

What is the equivalent of Stand-in for human agency?

When automated risk assessment becomes uncertain, what minimum capabilities must legitimate customers retain?

Who can challenge an automated restriction?

What independent process can restore access without simply repeating the original automated decision?

And who has the authority to decide when protecting customers has begun preventing them from conducting ordinary life?

Those questions cannot be answered by fraud-detection accuracy alone.

They require institutions to define what their defensive systems must preserve, not merely what they must prevent.

The bank's AI becomes more sophisticated.

The criminal searches for new weaknesses. The bank closes them.

Every defensive improvement changes the environment the criminal encounters. Every criminal adaptation changes the environment the bank must defend.

The interaction can become an arms race in which the people most affected have little influence over either side's objectives.

The criminal doesn't ask customers for permission to attack.

The bank may have legal and contractual authority to impose restrictions, but customers generally do not participate in every automated risk decision.

And the customer standing at the grocery checkout has no practical way to negotiate with either AI.

This is where the issue becomes larger than fraud.

Institutions can gradually transfer more decision authority to automated systems because doing so appears efficient, consistent, responsive, and protective.

But the ability of an individual to challenge those decisions may not improve at the same rate.

The danger is not that defensive AI must become overly restrictive.

It is that institutions may find increasing restrictions easier to justify than preserving meaningful human autonomy.

Especially when a malicious adversary keeps supplying new reasons to tighten the controls.

Much of the discussion about AI governance begins with whether systems behave as intended.

But our Nigerian Prince illustrates why it is insufficient.

The criminal's AI may be aligned with a malicious human intention.

The bank's AI may be aligned with a legitimate but incomplete institutional objective.

The interaction between them may produce consequences that neither system is required to recognize as a violation of its assigned task.

Governance must therefore examine more than the accuracy, reliability, or obedience of individual agents.

It must examine the consequences of their interaction.

For a bank deploying increasingly autonomous defenses, I would begin with three tests.

1. Measure the legitimate activity prevented.

Fraud detection should be evaluated alongside confirmed legitimate transactions denied or delayed, verification failures, and time required to restore access.

Those measures belong in the same governance conversation as fraud losses and detection performance.

Otherwise, a security improvement can conceal a deterioration in the service it exists to protect.

2. Test defensive behavior under adversarial pressure.

Security testing should examine whether malicious activity can provoke disproportionate restrictions while the defensive system continues following its approved rules.

This is different from asking whether an attacker can bypass the system.

The question is whether an attacker can manipulate its legitimate responses to produce harmful outcomes.

The test must evaluate the interaction, not merely the integrity of each individual component.

3. Preserve an accountable route to recovery.

Customers need a meaningful way to challenge prolonged or disproportionate restrictions.

An independent review process should have sufficient authority to reassess an automated decision rather than simply reproduce it.

That recovery route must itself be secured against abuse. Restoring human discretion cannot mean abandoning fraud controls.

The institution must deliberately balance both obligations.

These are proposed governance checks, not claims that a single set of controls will solve every possible adversarial interaction. They require testing against real operating conditions.

An autonomous system should not be permitted to redefine an institution's underlying purpose simply because a narrower objective becomes easier to optimize.

Nor should an institution treat every successful execution of an authorized policy as evidence that the policy remains appropriate.

Authority must remain accountable to the human purpose that justified granting it.

The distinction matters because the most consequential failures may not appear in conventional incident reports.

Its responses may be technically correct.

And its customers may be losing practical control over their own lives.

We tend to imagine an AI takeover as a dramatic event.

Machines become self-aware. They reject human authority. They seize control.

We deploy autonomous systems to make life easier.

Vulnerability justifies additional protection.

Protection justifies greater automated control.

And greater control can deepen dependence.

No system needs to decide that humanity is obsolete.

Institutions may simply continue delegating authority to systems that perform their assigned tasks more efficiently than people can.

The Nigerian Prince adds an uncomfortable twist.

A deliberately malicious actor may learn to exploit that delegation, provoking legitimate institutions into taking actions that restrict the very people they exist to serve.

The attacker doesn't have to win a contest against the bank's AI.

He may only need to make the bank's AI win the wrong contest.

And when you're standing at the grocery checkout, trying to use your own money, the distinction between malicious interference and legitimate protection may become increasingly difficult to appreciate.

The Nigerian Prince hasn't stolen your money.

He's helped convince your bank that you cannot be trusted to access it.

AI may not take control because it turns against humanity.

It may take control because we keep authorizing it to protect us from one another, until protection becomes indistinguishable from control.

AI Doesn't Have to Make Things Up to Mislead You

#9590. Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities

Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

#9588. BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.

🤗 Model (safetensors)  |  📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4)

We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement.

BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).

Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.

We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.

Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).

Learning from rules and environments (RL stages)

Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.

The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.

Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.

BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).

Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model.

Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.

Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1).

BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).

BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ.

Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70).

On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks.

Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14).

BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.

Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each.

Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9):

It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks.

BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.

BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.

[1] Yu, Qiying, et al. "DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025): 113222–113244.

[2] Zhang, Shaokun, et al. "Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1: Exploring Tool-Using Language Models with Reinforced Reasoning." International Conference on Learning Representations (2026).

[3] Qian, Cheng, et al. "ToolRL: Reward is All Tool Learning Needs." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025).

#9587. How long can butter sit out?: For the best baking success, here's the deal on saving softened butter for later.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions.

Ryan from our Baker’s Hotline is here with the answer.

You sure can! It will still work the next time you want to bake. But remember, as with any dairy product, there are always precautions to take.

The USDA recommends keeping butter at room temperature for no more than two days to prevent spoilage. Salt is a preservative and can lengthen the shelf life, but for the sake of this article, we’re talking about unsalted butter. (It’s more appropriate for baking and is the type called for in most King Arthur recipes.)

“If the butter has only been on the counter at room temperature for a few hours or overnight and has maintained a temperature below 70°F, it should be just fine to place back in the fridge,” says Ryan. “You may not notice a difference in the performance of the butter when you eventually use it, other than the wrapper being a bit wet or soft. Food safety-wise, it’s still good to use.”

“If the butter became very soft or started to melt during its time on the counter (or in the microwave if you were speeding up the process), you can put it back in the fridge, but it may not be the best to use in your recipe,” Ryan suggests. “You may notice when it solidifies that it’s separated or grainy. The water, fats, and solids in butter are an emulsion, which can break when melted and re-solidified.” If your recipe depends on butter to create air or structure, like a cake that calls for creaming butter and sugar, you’ll want to start over with new butter.

“If you used that butter in a recipe requiring creaming, the air you incorporate wouldn’t be as stable since the structure of the butter has changed,” Ryan says. “Your baked goods may not rise properly, and frostings may be soft and loose. Is it still safe to use? Food safety-wise, yes. But structure-wise, perhaps not.”

That butter can still be used for other things though! Extra-softened or even melted and re-solidified butter will still work perfectly to spread on toast or pancakes, to be made into brown butter, or to remelt and use in recipes calling for melted butter like a Graham Cracker Crust.

If your butter has been unrefrigerated for more than two days, you run the risk of it going rancid. As Ryan says, “There is no coming back from rancid butter.” It has a distinctly unpleasant flavor and a noticeable rancid smell that carries over into baked goods. It’s best to dispose of the butter if this happens.

But what if you want to keep your butter at room temperature for days at a time to slather on your morning toast? Ryan recommends storing your butter in a butter keeper if you want to leave it on the counter. “The water in the base of the jar creates an airtight seal, helping prevent the butter from spoiling. So long as it is stored away from direct heat and light, the butter in a container like this will be fine for a few days. Be sure to replace the water often and clean the container before filling again.”

“When working with butter in a recipe, I like to bring out and soften only the amount that is needed for what I am working on. That way, I don’t end up with extra butter that won’t be used right away,” he says. “Repeatedly moving butter from the fridge to the counter and then back invites spoilage and poor performance.”

In a rush? To soften your butter more quickly, Ryan advises, “Cut your butter into pats and place them on a plate in a single layer at room temperature. More surface area means that the butter will soften a bit faster!”
