#9460. COVID-19 and Moral Injury: a Mental Health Pandemic for Frontline Health Care Workers

More than 2 years ago, the alarm and first warnings of a global pandemic sounded. Now with over 830,000 deaths caused by COVID-19 in the US, there looms on the horizon a second underlying curve with equally serious long-term consequences: a mental health pandemic.

The mental health fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic demands recognition, intervention, and mitigation strategies. Among the many at-risk populations are frontline health care workers who have been at the epicenter of the global pandemic, working long shifts with at times a tenuous safety net and limited support, and caring for COVID-19 patients with limited resources, mixed messaging, and uncertainty with regards to an end to the crisis. The psychological effects in some health care providers are akin to the moral trauma or moral injury that is recognized in combat veterans with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Mental health professionals and other health care providers caring for frontline health care workers who present with insomnia, depression, anxiety, panic attacks, PTSD, and suicidal thoughts should recognize and validate their experiences and moral injury. Intervention strategies including health promotion, resilience training, and ongoing multilevel support will play an important role in flattening the moral injury curve.

As a rule, the frontline health care workforce is considered capable, competent, resilient, professional, and persevering in the face of adversity. However, COVID-19 presented as an unprecedented crisis unlike any other unforeseen disaster, eliciting fear, uncertainty, and anxiety, coupled with grief and loss, both personally and professionally.1 As noted by Warren D. Taylor, MD, MHSc, and Jennifer Urbano Blackford, PhD1:

The pandemic created anxiety and fear in health care providers, from physicians and nurses to allied health professionals and first-line responders. We fear for the safety of our families and patients. We grieve for those who have died. We feel guilt for not being able to save all our patients, for getting sick ourselves, and for abandoning our families. Many adopted the phrase, “we will get through this together but none of us will survive unscathed.”

At the outset, the shortage of equipment and resources, changing practice guidelines, and unpredictability of the workload rendered health care workers with a sense of powerlessness and loss of control of the conditions under which they were able to deliver care. The emotional distress and social isolation from family and friends exacted an immeasurable toll on the physical health and emotional well-being of the workforce, setting the stage for the inevitable moral injury.2

Moral injury is a term that has been applied to veterans of combat. Moral injury or moral distress as experienced by frontline health care providers occurs when health care providers are forced to make decisions that transgress their professional commitment to patient comfort and care, and forcibly shift their moral compass. They are not able to meet the physical, emotional, and end-of-life needs of patients.3

Watson et al noted that moral injury in health care workers “can occur when someone engages in, fails to prevent, or witnesses acts that conflict with their values or beliefs.”4 Moral injuries may result from the following, according to Watson et al4:

The consequences of such experiences may include feelings of rage, guilt, shame, and anger and moral injury is the “lasting psychological, spiritual, behavioral or social impact that may result from these experiences.”4 The number of acutely ill COVID-19 patients and high death rate coupled with lack of resources and at times rationing of limited resources such as personal protective equipment (PPE) and ventilators added to the dilemma that frontline health care workers faced.

In a study of 448 Jordanian nurses during the COVID-19 pandemic, the majority of nurses (64%) reported experiencing acute stress disorder (ASD) and 41% reported significant psychological distress, with a predilection for younger nurses compared to older nurses.5 However, coping self-efficacy was a protective factor with the potential to mitigate the severity of psychological distress.5 An online survey of nonhealth care providers (N=976) found that individuals with previous trauma were at highest risk for increased symptoms of anxiety, depression, and PTSD related to COVID-19 compared with individuals with no previous history of trauma.6

The long-term mental health consequences of moral injury for frontline health care workers have important implications for workforce survivability and durability; however, research on this topic is lacking. In one of the few published studies on moral injury among health care providers, investigators looked at the thematic content of experiences reported by nurses following incidents meeting the contextual definition of moral injury (ie, events with unintended consequences, potentially causing patient harm or putting patients at risk for serious injury). The investigators found nurses reported experiencing “guilt, shame, spiritual–existential crisis, and loss of trust.”7

COVID-19 has presented difficult and untenable working conditions beyond the scope of the challenges frontline health care workers are prepared for professionally. Frontline health care workers have experienced conflict and distress over prioritizing patient care vs their own safety, protecting family members from infection, and the reality that the supplies, medications, and equipment needed to save a life were not always available or were being rationed. Because of high infectivity, morbidity, and mortality associated with the spread of the virus, frontline health care workers were often in the position to be the only person at the bedside at the end of life with patients who were separated from their families. This is not how families should experience the loss of a loved one.4

There is a body of research regarding the long-term effects of moral injury among combat soldiers.3 It is reasonable to expect that feelings of guilt, shame, anger, and self-recrimination stemming from moral injury in these soldiers may be similar to feelings experienced by frontline health care workers during the COVID-19 pandemic and that their experiences increase the risk for acute stress reactions with long-term consequences including increased incidence of depression, anxiety, substance abuse, PTSD, and suicide.4,8 Behavior changes including intrusive memories, avoidance of situations that are reminders of prior events, self-isolation, and potential triggers of traumatic memories are common in individuals suffering from acute stress disorder or PTSD. Additional responses to stress, trauma, and moral injury include disturbed sleep, emotional changes such as numbing, desensitization, depersonalization, and a decreased capacity for empathy and compassion. For some individuals, the consequences of moral injury may be an opportunity for reflection and reprioritization of values and an existential inner process of reflecting on what is important in life.4

Given the consequences of moral injury, it is important for mental health professionals and health care providers treating frontline health care providers to recognize and identify those experiences that have the potential for promoting resilience.9

An analysis of data from 2,579 frontline health care workers in New York City early on in the pandemic showed that key factors predictive of psychological resilience were positive emotions, self-efficacy, purpose in life, strong social support, and not engaging in maladaptive coping strategies (eg, substance abuse).9 Psychological resilience was described by the authors as, “the capacity to adapt and thrive while facing adversity or challenging circumstances,” leading to the question of how can institutions promote psychological resilience in frontline health care workers?9

Initiativespromoting psychological resilience are critical.10,11 Interventions identifying those at high risk for moral injury and in need of support in the form of psychological first-aid and psychotherapy have the potential of improving resilience. Kameno et al administered the short-form of the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale with 4 additional questions, 2 regarding sleep, 1 on appetite changes, and 1 on alcohol misuse, in health care workers during the pandemic.12 The researchers found that women and nurses had higher rates of affective symptoms compared to men and other medical staff, respectively. The researchers noted that early identification and psychotherapy may improve psychological resilience and reduce psychological distress in nurses at high risk for maladaptive coping.12

The need for institutional support, leadership support, education, and training is equally important. Leadership and management are challenged to identify those practices that address the needs of their respective health care workers.10 Survey findings on the expectations and needs of health care workers (physicians, nurses, advanced practice clinicians, residents, and fellows; N=69) during the first week of the pandemic at a single hospital identified the following 5 requests of their organization: hear me, protect me, prepare me, support me, and care for me.13 Management and leadership have the opportunity to promote resilience and show visible support for the health care workforce with unique initiatives to help reduce and mitigate the long-term consequences of moral injury and acute stress response.

Similar to triage protocols and models to meet emergent health care systems demands from unexpected disasters, there is a need for a multilayered mental health care response for frontline workers. Self-care and wellness initiatives have the potential to reduce the long-term consequences of moral injury. Ongoing support, skills training, psychoeducation, and wellness education regarding strategies to address and process the experiences of frontline health care workers are critical for healing the wounds of moral injury. Empathic sensitivity on the part of mental health providers and primary care providers is essential. Listening to “the story” and having the opportunity to process and reflect on the self-talk related to the experience of moral injury can lay the groundwork for healing.

Self-care needs should include the opportunity to seek out and have available a support system of peers and colleagues. All too often the experience of shame, guilt, and self-condemnation are obstacles to seeking self-help and lead to self-isolation. If allowed to process and reflect on those experiences, health care workers may be provided an opportunity for experiential growth and a redefinition of priorities personally and professionally.

Leaders in health care have the opportunity to create and foster a culture of open, nonjudgmental communication. In the face of unpredictable events such as the COVID-19 pandemic, natural disasters, and social and political unrest that impact health care delivery, strategies are available to promote mental health recovery and return to stability and wellness among frontline health care workers.

Catherine R. Judd, MS, PA-C, CAQ-Psy, DFAAPA, is an assistant clinical professor in the Department of Physician Assistant Studies at the School of Health Professions, The University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, Texas.

1. Taylor WD, Blackford JU. Mental health treatment for front-line clinicians during and after the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic: a plea to the medical community. Ann Intern Med. 2020;173(7):574-575. doi:10.7326/M20-2440

2. Hossain F, Clatty A. Self-care strategies in response to nurses’ moral injury during COVID-19 pandemic. Nurs Ethics. 2021;28(1):23-32. doi:10.1177/0969733020961825

3. Borges LM, Barnes SM, Farnsworth JK, Bahraini NH, Brenner LA. A commentary on moral injury among health care providers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Psychol Trauma. 2020;12(S1):S138-S140. doi:10.1037/tra0000698

#9457. Skip The Oven: This Easy Turkey Dinner Is Ready In Half The Time

With Thanksgiving just around the corner, many of us are gearing up to spend time with friends and family, and enjoy a delicious meal. For those who are hosting and doing the cooking, however, there is considerably more to the holiday. Aside from cleaning the house top to bottom, preparing a huge meal, including a whole turkey, can be stressful to say the least. Eschewing the turkey might take a major burden off your plate, but if you don't want to go fully historical with your Thanksgiving feast (the Plymouth settlers likely ate different game birds and venison) you might instead opt for oven-free, skillet-cooked turkey meatballs in a savory gravy.

Meatballs are an excellent option because you can stuff the flavors of Thanksgiving turkey and stuffing into them, minus the hours of cook time. In fact, if you consider a 20 pound turkey takes four to five hours to roast, and making turkey meatballs takes an hour, tops (depending on how long it takes you to roll them all out), you're saving yourself a lot of time. It also means your oven is completely free for all the delicious sides, like hopefully mistake-free green bean casserole and hot, pillowy rolls. Further, this is a great meal to pull out any time of the year when you want a Thanksgiving turkey-like dinner, without the fuss.

If you're looking for inspiration on what ingredients to use in your turkey meatballs, we have some suggestions (and it's worth noting that none of these ideas add any significant time to the meatball preparation). It's not the best idea to use straight ground turkey because it tends to be quite lean; as you can see in the video above, the creator also includes Italian sausage, which has much-needed fat to help keep the balls moist and tender. If you don't want to use sausage, though, you could take Ina Garten's advice and use prosciutto, or see if you can find ground turkey thighs, as opposed to breast meat, because it has a higher fat content.

Of course to get that real Thanksgiving dinner taste, you'll also want to use plenty of herbs. Sage has a savory, meaty flavor that will boldly season those meatballs, while thyme adds warmth and earthiness; both are often used in stuffing, and they'll pair nicely with your ground turkey and sausage as well. A little rosemary brings a peppery, piney flavor into the mix, and parsley brightens with its herbaceousness.

For a sweet spin that adds another element of a popular Thanksgiving dish, toss in some dried cranberries that have been diced into little bits as well, or try pomegranate-infused Craisins. A touch of citrus zest, too, incorporates some sweetness and complexity.

#9455. Give Grilled Cheese A Major Flavor And Protein Boost With One Hearty Addition

There are seemingly as many kinds of grilled cheese as there are individuals on this planet. There are, for example, plenty of international styles worth trying, while even the classic all-American versions can consist of a variety of cheeses, like American, cheddar, Gouda, and Havarti. You might like to make yours using mayonnaise on the bread, while your neighbor prefers butter in the pan. And then there are extra fillings and additions. Some people add a little bacon and maple syrup to their sandwiches, while others turn theirs into a breakfast masterpiece with an egg. Another fantastically tasty option is to add chili, which not only imbues the meal with a huge dose of extra flavor, but also gives you a nice protein boost.

Whether you have more leftover chili than you know what to do with, or a can or two in your pantry collecting dust, it's actually the perfect addition. It's savory, hearty, and saucy, which works so well when layered with cheese (which chili often gets topped with) and sandwiched between two slices of bread, pan-browned to crispy perfection. And if you have daily protein goals, a ¼ cup of chili, which is a reasonable starting quantity for a single sandwich, can typically get you roughly 4 to 5 grams closer to meeting that target (though this will vary depending on the recipe).

One of the best things about chili grilled cheese sandwiches is how easy they are to make. You can assemble them in the pan like normal, but add a scoop of chili onto one slice of bread before closing it up. This works well if you're just making one or two sandwiches, but if you have more mouths to feed, you can actually make a whole bunch in the oven at once. You'll just want to be sure to spread butter on the outside of each slice of bread, combine your chili with plenty of shredded cheese to make a gooey, melty filling, and then flip the sandwiches halfway through baking so both sides get nice and toasty.

Now, like all grilled cheeses, this variation is still quite customizable. For example, if you wanted to add some sharpness to help cut through all the richness of the other ingredients, you could sprinkle green onion on top of the chili. Alternatively, if you wanted a bite, plus a bit of spice, sliced or chopped jalapeños would do nicely (or you might make the sweet pickled version known as cowboy candy). To amp up the protein even more, some bacon wouldn't be out of place, either. You could also lean into the idea of a chili cheese dog grilled cheese, and slice a hot dog lengthwise, fry it up, and place that on top of the chili layer.

#9453. Skip Butter And Milk: The Canned Ingredient That Makes Burgers Juicier

Juicy burger patties are all about nailing the perfect ratio of fat, moisture, and protein for something that isn't wet or greasy but also isn't dry and crumbly. While butter and milk can certainly help, condensed cream of mushroom soup is a far better and easier alternative that perfectly strikes the balance when you use the right amount.

Cream of mushroom soup may be billed as a shelf-stable meal in its own right, but the condensed version is a canned soup hack for many recipes thanks to its texture and flavor. It's had much of its moisture removed and therefore has a higher ratio of fat. While wet enough to infuse proteins with a bit of juiciness, its fat content helps preserve the tenderness and protect the existing moisture, all with the delicious umami of mushrooms. Condensed varieties also tend to be more potent, so the small amount you'll use for juiciness translates into a subdued but still noticeable taste.

Chopped mushrooms for extra-juicy burgers is an increasingly common tactic, but evenly mixing all the little bits without overworking the meat is challenging. While wet ingredients are far easier to thoroughly disperse, they come with a caveat. You need a starch to hold and release the moisture unless you want it to drip out right away. Breadcrumbs are a common choice in meatballs and other ground beef recipes, and a ratio of half a cup of starch to one 10.5-ounce can to one pound of protein gets the job done quite well.

Burger patties made with condensed cream of mushroom soup are pretty forgiving and more difficult to dry out, but that doesn't mean you can just chuck them on the grill willy-nilly. To preserve the juiciness and keep them easy to work with, you need to know when to leave them alone, whether that's while they're raw, cooking, or resting.

Immediately cooking a burger infused with condensed cream of mushroom soup leaves a lot of surface moisture. This ends up steaming it, so it doesn't develop a good crust and robs it of much of the juice you were attempting to preserve. Letting any patty chill in the fridge helps it firm up and makes it easier to manipulate on the grill, but it also allows the breadcrumbs to absorb the moisture to release later. Similar to marinating, it also helps to let the flavors mix a bit, so you don't end up with pockets of intense mushroom-ness that can ruin an otherwise good bite.

While exact timing varies based on your method, the 5-6-7 rule when cooking burgers is a reliable starting point. Five minutes on one side, six on the other, then seven minutes resting helps you balance enough heat to create a crust with enough time to ensure that the insides are not still raw. The resting is particularly important, as you don't want to release all your juice onto your plate or as steam and make your subsequent bites drier.

#9452. The best Thanksgiving baking tips from Ina Garten, Erin McDowell, and more pro bakers: Top tips from the Things Bakers Know podcast.

It’s the most wonderful baking season of the year, and to help you bake your best, we have top tips from some of the country’s best bakers, pulled from conversations on the Things Bakers Know podcast. Below, you’ll find Thanksgiving strategies from upcoming podcast guests Ina Garten (episode dropping November 23!) and King Arthur’s Martin Philip (find his episode November 16), as well as guests from previously aired episodes, including Erin McDowell, Helen Goh, and many more of our baking friends.

“The one thing I think people think they can do is multiply a recipe times four and think it’s going to come out fine, which it won’t,” Ina shared on her forthcoming podcast episode. Instead of taking one recipe and just multiplying by three or four, she suggests either baking the original recipe multiple times, or doubling it and baking two or three times, depending on how many people you’re feeding. Just don’t multiply more than once! If you do, the leavening and flavoring starts to get thrown off.

If you’re baking for a lot of people, Ina also suggests making recipes scaled for a baking sheet. As she explains, “It’s easier to bake, and it’s easier to cut.” We’d recommend Slab Chocolate Pecan Pie, Pumpkin Cake Bars with Cream Cheese Frosting, or Walnut and Oat Slab Pie.

While you may be excited to try out a show-stopping recipe from a brand-new cookbook, Ina recommends resisting temptation. “You don’t want to test something you haven’t made a million times,” she cautions. “Even for me, it adds enormous stress.” Instead of turning to a first-time recipe, Ina highly recommends that you “do the things you know will come out perfectly every time.” And if you do want to make a new-to-you recipe this Thanksgiving, consider baking it once or twice in the weeks leading up to the holiday, so you have the chance to practice and work out any kinks (like figuring out make-ahead components or fridge storage) before hosting on the big day.

No one wants a soggy bottom on their pie, especially a super-juicy one like apple pie. Erin McDowell has lots of tips to avoid a soggy bottom, but her biggest one is to precook your apple filling before assembling your pie. “We can't necessarily predict how juicy any given fruit is, so even if you're using the same apple … each time, they are going to be a little bit different,” she explained on our podcast episode all about apples. Precooking the filling allows you to adjust based on the juiciness of the fruit you’re using that day. “If you're dealing with not-very-juicy apples, you may not have to cook it as long. If they're really juicy, you may have to cook it longer, but the process is the same.”

Pie crust can be incredibly intimidating for some bakers. But pie queen Stacey Mei Yan Fong says the key to success is sometimes to chill out, figuratively and literally. “The best thing you can do is just chill, as in calm down. You're not doing brain surgery,” she reminded Jessica in our Thanksgiving pie episode. “And also use your fridge!” As she points out, “the minute things start getting too wet or things start getting too warm, that's when people panic.” So take a moment to chill the dough and make it easier to work with. If the butter's getting soft or your pie dough is getting difficult to work with, just put it in the fridge to cool down for 10 to 15 minutes.

It’s not just the fridge, either — your freezer can also be incredibly helpful. Stacey likes to freeze her pies before baking, which she says helps the crimping hold its shape as it bakes. And remember that, as Stacey points out, “Pie is kind of a lesson in patience.”

On our special Holiday Q+A Extravaganza dropping November 23, King Arthur’s Director of Baking Education Amber Eisler has a crucial tip for avoiding runny apple pies — make sure you see your pie filling actively bubbling through the vents in your pie crust. As she explains, “It means the filling has boiled and bubbled, so the starches in the filling are actually thickening, which is a super important part of [avoiding a soupy pie].”

There’s a lot of cooking and baking happening around Thanksgiving, which means your oven can get pretty crowded, pretty quickly. But be wary of overfilling it. Even though your oven may have up to three racks inside, Martin Philips cautions against using them all at the same time. “Don’t make the mistake of crowding the oven when it comes to rolls. Let bread have its moment,” he says. Bake your pies the day before to save oven space; a turkey, too will stay hot out of the oven for hours. When baking rolls, you want “top and bottom heat, use your convection setting, make sure that air is moving,” says Martin. “Guard the rolls, y’all!”

Cookbook author and professional psychologist Helen Goh believes in the power of baking to bring meaning and fulfillment to our lives. During this busy holiday season, full of messy kitchens, family squabbles, lengthy to-do lists, and lots of hosting, it can be easy to get overwhelmed. But baking can actually be a calming, comforting activity right now. “Some people say baking makes them nervous because you have to focus,” says Helen. But part of the therapeutic effect of baking comes from forcing us to focus on a single task at hand. As she points out, “that takes you away from all that white noise about what you did yesterday or what's going to happen tomorrow,” and instead allows you to live mindfully in the moment.

Happy Thanksgiving from all of us here at King Arthur. If you run into baking troubles or just need a little support in the kitchen, our Baker’s Hotline is here to help.

#9429. Does β‑Blocker Use Increase Depression Risk?

The association between β-blocker use and depression was investigated in a population-based observational study recently published in the journal Drug Safety.

While depression is often cited as an adverse effect of β-blocker use, there is limited evidence supporting this causal relationship. To better understand the association between beta blockers and the risk of new-onset depression, the study authors analyzed data from the UK population-based Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) GOLD database.

“We identifed patients aged 18-80 years with an incident depression diagnosis between 2000 and 2016, and matched controls, and estimated the risk (odds ratio [OR]) of depression in association with use of β-blockers,” the study authors explained.

Findings of the analysis revealed an increased risk of developing depression among short-term users of β-blockers compared with no use at all (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.91; 95% CI, 1.72-2.12).

Among short-term users, increased risk of depression was mainly restricted to patients with a neuropsychiatric disorder taking propranolol (aOR 6.33, 95% CI 5.16–7.76).  Patients on propranolol for a cardiovascular indication were found to be at slightly elevated risk of depression (aOR 1.44, 95% CI 1.14–1.82). Apart from propranolol, no other lipophilic β-blocker or hydrophilic β-blocker was found to increase the risk of depression.

Additionally, no association was observed between long-term use of β-blockers and the risk of depression (aOR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.85-0.94).

“Our findings suggest that the reported association between use of β-blockers and depression may not be causal but rather a result of protopathic bias,” the study authors concluded.

Bornand D, Reinau D, Jick SS, Meier CR. β‑blockers and the risk of depression: A matched case–control study. Drug Safety. Published online January 19, 2022. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40264-021-01140-5.

Pan-fried chicken. Luscious, savory Cajun cream sauce. Homemade mashed potatoes. Green beans. Apple crisp for dessert.

I served it in deep bowls and we let the girls eat on the living room floor, using the coffee table as their table, while we watched American Ninja Warrior together with the windows open – which, frankly, is the move of two parents who are feeling extra generous and a little out of their mind with the joys of early fall weather. But that meal will be a top 5 meal for me this year, for sure. We all devoured in silence and then cozied up with full bellies to watch some ridiculous TV together.

Here’s an idea I keep coming back to: shrimp. Like what if you just made the sauce, and then threw a pound of uncooked jumbo shrimp in there? It would poach right in the sauce! I haven’t been able to pull myself away from the chicken and mashed potatoes combination, but I feel shrimp should at least be considered.

Hope this recipe gives you all same cozy fall feelings it gave me.

Also a big fan of using the air fryer here, if you’re not feeling the pan-frying.

This picture shows the shallots minced; I also really love to do this with a thinly sliced shallot, sliced on a mandoline. The shape will give you these little ribbons through the sauce.

Add cream and broth, and simmer till it’s GLORIOUS.

I mean, showstopper material right there.

My favorite combo for serving is mashed potatoes and green beans. LIGHTS OUT. So good.

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

Pan-fried chicken in a luscious Cajun cream sauce, served with mashed potatoes and green beans – loving this easy, cozy weeknight dinner!

To air fry the chicken: Air fry at 375 for 10-12 minutes, or until at least 165 degrees internal temperature.

Roasted Potatoes and Broccoli (Oven): Toss 3-4 cups halved baby potatoes with avocado oil and salt on a sheet pan. Roast the potatoes at 425 for 15 minutes. Scoot the potatoes over, add 3-4 cups broccoli and ¼ cup water to the same sheet pan, and roast for another 15 minutes.

Roasted Potatoes and Broccoli (Air Fryer): Toss 2 cups halved baby potatoes with avocado oil and salt. Air fry at 375 for 12 minutes. Add 2 cups frozen or fresh broccoli; air fry at 400 for another 10-12 minutes.

Keywords: cajun chicken, chicken dinner, mashed potatoes

#9421. 36 Healthy Fall Dinners With All The Cozy

Healthy and nourishing fall dinners that are super cozy, too! Some of my favorite bowls, salads, soups, and more!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 18, 2026

Fall dinners are here, and honestly, this is the kind of food I wait for all year. Steamy bowls, creamy sauces, roasted veggies, cozy spices, and meals that make the whole house smell amazing. These healthy fall recipes bring all the sweater-weather comfort while still being nourishing enough for an everyday weeknight!

To call out a few of my all-time favorites from this list:

Nourishing food should still feel generous, cozy, and completely delicious, and these dinners are it!

Roasted sweet potatoes topped with creamy chipotle sauce, spicy ground chicken, avocado, cilantro, and pickled onion. My family loves them!

I love this Kale Apple Salad! Kale, brussels sprouts, rosemary cashews, apples, fried bread cheese, crispy shallots, and crisp apple maple dressing!

Silky carrot soup topped with spiced ground beef and toasty pine nuts! Bright, savory, warming, all the best things!

Amazingly creamy, saucy chickpea curry served over rice with a dollop of chili crisp and a side of cucumber salad. Ready in 20 minutes!

One of my family’s favorite easy dinners that works SO well for meal prep! Sweet potatoes and ground beef get dolloped with a creamy high protein street corn style dip that is bonkers delicious.

Detox Crockpot Lentil Soup – a clean and simple soup made with onions, garlic, carrots, olive oil, squash, and LENTILS! Super healthy and easy to make.

The BEST Grain Bowl! Roasted root vegetables, earthy grains, dried fruit, dark leafy greens, buttery goat cheese, and lusciously creamy balsamic dressing.

Coconut Curry Salmon! Broiled salmon with a salty-sweet spice rub, creamy coconut curry sauce, and steamy rice to soak it all up.

These tempeh bowls are a true fall favorite! Massaged kale, sweet potatoes, roasty marinated maple-mustard tempeh, crunchy apple, and an unexpected pile of briney sauerkraut.

Lemongrass, ginger, shallot, and the brightness of lime! These broth bowls have got it all – luscious broth, fluffy rice, protein, and fresh herbs.

Saucy shredded chicken, yellow rice, pickled onions, greens, and cilantro pesto on top. It’s a flavor and color delight!

We are living our best bowl life this week. Seasoned sweet potato wedges and chicken meatballs or rotisserie chicken all piled onto a plate with a little puddle of punchy green avocado mojo sauce. Yes, wow, repeat.

This 7-Layer Beet Salad is a stunner! Studded with cooked beets, supremed oranges, chopped pistachios, creamy truffle ricotta, and a bit of fresh mint. So fresh, so good!

These House Favorite Brussels Sprouts are the best side veg and are speckled with bright bursts of cranberries and nutty walnuts. The perfect addition to any meal!

These Spicy Peanut Tofu Bowls are a meal prep / weeknight dinner life-saver! Crispy tofu, roasted veggies, fluffy rice, and a spicy sweet peanut sauce all over top.

These beauties need to be on your table! Deeply roasted rainbow carrots, swizzles of tangy garlicky yogurt sauce, a golden drizzle of honey, and festive pistachio crunches on top.

Healing Chicken and Rice Soup that is limey, salty, and so fresh! Garlic-ginger-infused broth, shredded chicken thighs, tender jasmine rice, fresh herbs, and peanuts. YUM.

Brussels & Kale Caesar! Papery-thin shreds of brussels sprouts and chopped lacinato kale, tossed with a creamy, garlicky, avocado-based vegan caesar dressing, topped off with the most addicting cheezy garlic croutons.

Autumn Glow Salad with Lemon Dressing – a MUST for healthy, glowy eating! Roasted cauliflower, sweet potato, grains, and apples.

Healthy and versatile bowls that come together under a generous drizzle of addictingly creamy vegan chipotle tahini sauce.

A savory coconut creamy broth, swirls of chili oil floating on top, beautiful veg and cubes of flavor-soaked tofu, and a pile of steamy rice at your service.

A cozy, hearty, humble bowl of this Country Chicken Stew is waiting for you! Chicken, thick-cut bacon, navy beans, veggies, and fresh herbs all simmering in one big pot. It’s a good one, friends!

This Hot Honey Salmon is giving off major fancy-to-eat-but-not-fancy-to-make vibes. Spicy-sweet salmon coated in fresh garlic, stone ground mustard, sweet honey, and flecks of red peppers flakes. It’s a magical little number!

Harissa Chickpeas with Whipped Feta! Perfectly spicy/saucy/tomato-y chickpeas smothered in creamy, garlicky whipped feta and served with naan, lemons, and cucumbers. Your next weeknight wonder!

Easy Veggie Enchiladas! Saucy, cheese, filling, cozy, and packed with any roasted veggies you want. Super versatile and easy to make!

Guess what’s for dinner? Creamy, spicy, delicious red curry lentils, made in the Instant Pot.

Amazing Mushroom Bowls with Kale Pesto! Smoky, sweet, salt mushrooms (or tempeh!), caramelized pineapple, peppers, and dollop of kale pesto, all served over rice.

Sesame Beef and Broccoli! Full of protein, green broccoli goodness, and sticky-sweet garlic and ginger flavor. Perfect at-home takeout!

Creamy Thai Sweet Potato Curry – packed with nutrition! Our favorite easy, healthy, winter comfort food recipe.

These Roasted Cauliflower Hummus Bowls are LIFE-CHANGING. A bed of garlicky creamy hummus, piled high with spiced roasted cauliflower, and a speckling of fresh lemony tomatoes and herbs.

Spicy Shrimp with Cauliflower Mash and Garlic Kale – tender-sweet shrimp and smoky garlic kale over creamy cauliflower mash. The most DELICIOUS fake-fancy weeknight dinner!

Roasted Vegetable Bowls! Crispy tender roasted veggies, buttery avocado, all together in a bowl with a drizzle of green tahini sauce.

15 Minute Meal Prep Cilantro Lime Chicken and Lentils! The BEST easy protein powerhouse meal prep. Just 15 mins of prep and totally hands-off cooking!

Instant Pot Sweet Potato Tortilla Soup! A smoky, limey, tomato-rich broth with onion, garlic, jalapeño, crispy tortilla strips, and tender chunks of sweet potato.

These healthy chipotle sweet potato skins are stuffed with a chipotle-sweet potato filling, black beans, corn, and topped with cheese. SO GOOD.

Healing Bowls: turmeric sweet potatoes, brown rice, red quinoa, arugula, poached egg, lemon dressing.

Fall is for snacking, too! Here are some of my favorite healthy snacks – for myself, or for my kids’ lunchboxes!

#9419. The Elephant in the Rheum – “Burnout” Among the Workforce

Feelings of stress, fatigue, and exhaustion – what is being described as “burnout” – have become a common occurrence among providers, including rheumatologists, with important implications in clinical practice. Various surveys and studies have reported a substantial prevalence of burnout (approximately 50%) among rheumatology providers.

Beth L. Jonas, MD, Reeves Foundation Distinguished Professor of Medicine and chief of the Division of Rheumatology, Allergy, and Immunology at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (UNC), joins us on this episode to provide deeper insight on the issue of “burnout” from a clinical practice standpoint.

Read the full transcript of the episode here.

Beth L. Jonas, MD, is the Reeves Foundation Distinguished Professor of Medicine and chief of the Division of Rheumatology, Allergy, and Immunology at UNC.

A recipient of a 2015 Rheumatology Research Foundation (RRF) Clinician Scholar Educator Award, Dr Jonas has developed a novel curriculum in Rheumatology in the Foundation Phase at UNC. She is a clinician educator and has an active rheumatology practice, where she sees patients with a wide spectrum of inflammatory rheumatic disorders. She teaches rheumatology to medical students, residents, and fellows and is actively involved in curricular development to train both physicians and advance practice providers in rheumatology.

Dr Jonas currently serves on the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Workforce Solutions Committee. She has previously served as the chair of the ACR Committee on Training and Workforce and has served as co-chair of the ACR In-Training Examination Taskforce. She has served on the board of the Rheumatology Research Foundation as well as the RRF Scientific Advisory Committee.

Dr Jonas is a founding member of the Carolinas Fellows Collaborative (CFC), a group of program directors from the Carolinas who work to enhance the education of their collective trainees. Dr Jonas was honored as the ACR Distinguished Rheumatology Program Director in 2015.

This article originally appeared on Rheumatology Advisor

Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.

#9418. Apple Crisp

My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 29, 2026

Made this last night, and it’s now the whole family’s favorite apple crisp. Easy to make and very, very delicious!

I jotted this apple crisp recipe into the notes app in my phone several years ago, and I return to it every fall.

Jammy, cinnamon-scented apples baked under a heavy (and I do mean heavy) blanket of buttery crumble.

I remember first making this in our old kitchen for a late-October dinner party – I made wild rice soup and apple cider old fashioneds (unreal), and someone pulled out the guitar just as the smell of apple crisp was floating from the oven. Absolutely charmed. I obviously bonded with this specific apple crisp that night and it has been with me ever since.

Why it’s good, if you ask me: the caramely apple layer underneath gets properly jammy, the topping gets properly crisp – just enough to provide contrast, AND, and, and, where the two layers melt together in the middle is just pure fall magic. Soft, buttery, and delicious.

Apple crisp in general is very simple, and this one feels rustic, almost, especially if you make it in a cast iron pan, which I usually do. Is she making apple crisp or is she living out her dreams from Little House on the Prairie on a chilly fall night? We’ll never know.

Toss apples with sugar, cinnamon, and flour. This photo shows apples that have been thinly sliced on a mandoline. You can also dice them! Both delicious.

I stir it up with a spoon or fork, and then bring it together into crumbles with my hands.

It’ll turn into a beautiful golden crumble with a layer of jammy apples underneath.

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!

This can work with or without peeling the apples. Personally, I don’t peel the apples – I am lazy, and I just can’t be bothered to mess with what is already a perfectly good fruit. The peels cook down the same way the apples do, so they become soft and unobtrusive in the apple crisp.

Keywords: apple crisp, classic apple crisp, apple crisp recipe, fall dessert

#9417. Pastina Soup (Italian Penicillin)

This soup is my new go-to when my family is sick. The broth here is AMAZING – light, flavorful, and nourishing. Absolute comfort food.

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 1, 2026

What an awesome soup recipe! The family loved it! It will be on repeat in our home especially with the kids asking for more!!! Thank you.

Like, slurp that savory broth and go back for a third bowl kind of good.

My daughter got sick last week, which means that our whole family got sick last week. And when I get sick, I lose two things: 1) my appetite, and 2) my interest in cooking.

This pastina soup truly SAVED us last week. It is:

I can’t say enough about how much I loved this last week. I sat down at the table with a steamy bowl with extra parm on top, and found myself repeatedly going back for “just one more scoop” of the broth over those tiny stars, even though I swore I hadn’t been feeling hungry just a moment earlier.

My girls were pretty excited about eating tiny star pasta with olive oil + Parmesan, while Bjork and I ladled the luscious broth over our bowls and finally tucked into some nurturing food for the first time in several days.

Pastina refers to the tiny star shaped pasta, which I found at Target, and the nickname Italian Penicillin refers to the healing nature of the savory broth – almost like a chicken noodle soup, but simpler. (And if I’m being honest, I prefer this to chicken noodle.)

I hope you are healthy and well, physically and emotionally. But if you’re not, this is comfort meal that has been serving our family so well lately!

I keep them real chunky, and I give them a quick sauté with olive oil before adding all the liquid just to get things extra fragrant.

I use water and Better Than Bouillon broth base.

Transfer to a bowl to cool down for a moment.

And then add them right back to the broth pot.

Source Notes: “Italian penicillin” is a nickname for pastina soup, or pastina (small pasta) in broth. It is playfully compared to medicine because of its healing vibe, being that it is a warm, nostalgic, nourishing comfort food. It originated with generations of Italian grandmothers and it has moved into the spotlight after becoming a popular trend on TikTok over the last few years. 🙂

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

This soup has become my go-to recipe when my family is sick. The broth is amazing – simple, light, flavorful, and nourishing! It’s absolute comfort food.

Okay technically yes, I think you could! But here’s why I prefer not to:

– it will make the broth a bit thicker / starchier, and I prefer a silky, light broth

– the noodles will be more at risk of overcooking and getting mushy since they continue to sit in the hot liquid

– it doesn’t keep as well as leftovers (I prefer to just freeze the broth on its own)

– the experience of pouring the broth over the noodles is really fun. 🙂

#9416. Easy Eggplant Bolognese (1 Pot!)

Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!

When we add another bolognese to the blog (Yes, we already have versions 1, 2, 3, and 4), you know it’s something special! This newest version is made with EGGPLANT, meaning it’s the perfect bolognese for late summer. It’s light yet satisfying, creamy yet bright, and full of bold Italian-inspired flavor — everyone will be asking for seconds!

Even better? It’s a breeze to make — just 1 pot required! What are you waiting for? Get that pasta water boiling!

Bolognese is an Italian sauce that gets its name from the Italian city of Bologna. It’s typically made with meat, soffrito (onions, celery, and carrots), white wine, milk, and tomato paste or sauce, all simmered to create a rich, flavorful sauce.

Our eggplant version strays from the traditional as it excludes meat (and includes eggplant) and incorporates dairy alternatives. But the rest of the dish is very similar to traditional bolognese and feels so hearty it might convert even the most adamant veggie skeptics!

This 1-pot eggplant bolognese is everything you want for a cozy pasta night, minus the fuss! It starts with sautéing onion and carrots to create a simple, savory-sweet base. Next, we add eggplant (cut into very small cubes) and let it sauté until it has softened and browned (hello, flavor!).

Build the flavor even further with garlic and red pepper flakes and by deglazing the pan with wine. Crushed tomatoes and tomato paste ensure a bright, tomato-forward sauce, and a small amount of dairy-free milk (we like homemade cashew milk) gives it a gentle creaminess and richness. The final flavor touches include dried Italian herbs (basil + oregano), sea salt, and maple syrup to balance the acidity of the tomatoes.

Once all the ingredients are in your pan, it’s time to let the heat do its magic. Simmering for at least 20-30 minutes allows the sauce to thicken and concentrates the flavors as liquid evaporates away. If you have the time, you can let it continue simmering for up to an hour for even more flavor!

When it’s done simmering, you’ll be left with an oh-so delicious, plant-powered sauce perfect for serving with your favorite pasta! It would also be lovely over polenta and is elevated by garnishing with fresh basil and our homemade vegan parmesan cheese.

We think you’ll LOVE this eggplant bolognese! It’s:RichSavoryCreamy yet brightLight yet satisfyingEasy to make& SO delicious!

It’s the perfect dish for a late summer pasta night! While quick enough for a weeknight, it’s also impressive enough to serve to dinner guests, especially paired with our Simple Vegan Meatballs, Pesto Turkey Meatballs, or Chickpea Caesar Salad (30 Minutes!).

If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!

#9409. Fall Freezer Meals #2

These Fall Freezer Meals have been SO helpful for us. The prep is shockingly easy!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 14, 2026

A few months ago, I discovered what feels like a little life hack.

I started spending an hour each month getting a few meals prepped for the month ahead. We’re talking just assembling stuff for my favorite recipes into bags and freezing it!

And I can’t tell you how much this system makes me feel like I have my life together! It’s the best.

The recipes this month are absolute family favorites for fall!

And they all have cook times for Crockpot, Instant Pot, and stovetop methods. 🙂

Hope these help make your life easier this month like they have for us!

Everything you need is right on them. I print the cards out and attach them to the bags so I don’t have to use my phone at all for the prep or cooking.

For the streusel: mix 4 tablespoons melted butter, 1/3 cup brown sugar, and 3/4 cup flour into small crumbles.

Spray a muffin tin with avocado oil. Fill tins two-thirds of the way full with batter; top with streusel.

Store muffins in an airtight container or bag in the freezer (or fridge). To reheat from frozen, microwave 45-60 seconds.

Remove chicken from the sauce and shred. Blend sauce until smooth. Add chicken back in. Serve in tortillas with all the taco fixings you want!

Add 1-2 cups heavy cream and 1-2 cups chicken broth (as needed). To thicken: whisk 2 tbsp. cornstarch with 2 tbsp. cold water; add and simmer.

Whisk 1 1/2 tbsp. cornstarch in 1 1/2 tbsp. cold water; add to bubbling pot and let simmer until slightly thickened.

Stir in 2 cups of fresh spinach and fresh cilantro just before serving.

Serve with rice and chili crisp. I also love this with cucumber salad (thinly sliced cucumber and red onion, tossed with vinegar, avocado oil, salt, and sugar).

#9407. Cheesy Vegan Enchilada Skillet (30 Minutes!)

Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!

Everything you love about enchiladas, minus the fuss! This super flavorful, cheesy vegan enchilada skillet comes together in about 30 minutes with simple methods, minimal dishes, and no need to fill or roll tortillas.

This easy, nourishing dish features tender cubed sweet potato or winter squash, fiber- & protein-rich black beans, and a rich red enchilada sauce. Everything gets simmered in 1 pan and topped with a melty cashew “cheese” that makes it SUPER satisfying and delicious!

It’s believed that enchiladas may have originated from a similar Mayan dish called papadzules. But the first written recipe for enchiladas was in an 1831 cookbook called El Cocinero mexicano. Typically, enchiladas are made with meat, seafood, beans, cheese, potatoes, or vegetables stuffed in corn tortillas and topped with enchilada sauce.

Our “inspired-by” enchilada skillet has all the flavors of classic enchiladas, but it’s vegan, and instead of rolling the filling in tortillas, we slice the tortillas and cook everything together in one pan on the stovetop!

This 1-pan, 30-minute vegan enchilada skillet begins with a base of sautéed vegetables — onion, garlic, sweet potato, and poblano pepper. The veggies are flexible here, so feel free to experiment! We love kabocha squash for a fall variation and have found green bell peppers work well when poblanos aren’t available. We also think butternut squash would be nice, as would greens such as kale or spinach.

Once the onions are very tender and the squash and peppers are just beginning to soften, we stir in black beans + corn tortillas that have been sliced into strips.

Next comes the final ingredient in the skillet portion of this dish (hello, simple + flavorful!): red enchilada sauce. We love the bold flavor of our homemade enchilada sauce (and usually have it stocked in the freezer), but this recipe also works well with store-bought enchilada sauce.

And lastly, it just wouldn’t be enchiladas without: the CHEESE! More specifically, a flavorful cashew “cheese” sauce inspired by our fan favorite Cheesy Vegan Pizza Beans. It’s made by blending up cashews, water, lime juice, garlic, tapioca starch, and sea salt. When poured over the enchilada skillet and covered with a lid, the heat and tapioca starch do their magic, creating a melty, cheesy layer! Total swoon!

We highly recommend trying the cashew “cheese” sauce, even if you’re not vegan or dairy-free! It’s super easy and takes this dish to a whole new level. However, this enchilada skillet is also delicious with shredded vegan or dairy cheese (such as pepper jack).

We think you’ll LOVE this recipe! It’s:SmokySpicySuper flavorfulSatisfyingVersatileQuick & easy to make& SO delicious!

This dish is hearty and amazing as a standalone quick meal for weeknights! It would also pair well with our Smoky Shredded Tofu Taco “Meat” or 1-Pan Mexican Shredded Chicken for a higher-protein option. Or, for more veggies, try it with our Crunchy Jicama Slaw or Quick Citrusy Cabbage Slaw.

If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!

#9405. Warning Letters Sent to Online Pharmacies Illegally Selling Schedule II Stimulants

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) have issued joint warning letters to 2 websites for illegally selling and distributing or dispensing schedule II stimulants, including amphetamine drug products marketed as Adderall.

The warning letters to kubapharm.com and premiumlightsupplier.com state that the websites are selling amphetamine drug products, including Adderall, that are misbranded and in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Additionally, by failing to register the online pharmacies with the DEA, despite knowingly or intentionally advertising the sale of controlled substances, these websites are also in violation of the Ryan Haight Online Pharmacy Act.

“These letters are not only a warning to the companies that illegally sell prescription medications, but they also serve as a warning to consumers who have bought or have considered buying medications online without a legitimate prescription,” said DEA Administrator Anne Milgram. “Consumers cannot trust the safety or legitimacy of pills sold on unaccredited sites.”

In a press release, the Agency reinforced its commitment to stopping online operators illegally selling potentially harmful drug products to consumers. “These particular types of online pharmacies also undermine our efforts to help consumers safely purchase legitimate prescription medicines over the internet,” said FDA Commissioner Robert M. Califf, MD. “FDA will continue partnering with DEA in an effort to safeguard public health and protect consumers who need access to these important medicines.”

FDA and DEA warn online pharmacies illegally selling Adderall to consumers. News release. US Food and Drug Administration. Accessed April 12, 2022. https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/fda-and-dea-warn-online-pharmacies-illegally-selling-adderall-to-consumers-301524032.html

#9403. No-Bake Cranberry Orange Bliss Bites

Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!

Cozy, bright, and bursting with holiday flavor — these Cranberry Orange Bliss Bites are the perfect little treat when holiday baking season is in full swing and you’re out of time and energy. Inspired by Starbucks’ Bliss Bars, they pack the tart-sweet magic of cranberries and fresh orange zest into tender, no-bake bites you can whip up in minutes!

Even better? They’re vegan, gluten-free, and require zero baking — making them a lifesaver during the busy holiday season. A drizzle of white chocolate (or creamy coconut butter) makes them extra festive, but they’re just as delicious on their own. Let’s make bliss bites!

Besides tasting absolutely magical, these bliss bites get their name because they’re inspired by the legendary Bliss Bars from Starbucks (IYKYK!). The Starbucks bars have a chewy blondie base with cream cheese frosting, cranberries, white chocolate, and orange zest — total swoon!

The addition of orange juice + zest and dried cranberries kick things up a notch and sends them into Bliss Bar territory!

The final touch is an optional drizzle of melted white chocolate chips, coconut butter, or our favorite — a mix of the two! While the white chocolate creates a thicker, sweeter, and more decadent frosting, the coconut butter creates a drippier texture and adds a more pronounced coconut flavor that we enjoy. The combination is the best of both worlds!

We hope you LOVE these bites! They’re:ZestyBrightSweet with pops of tartnessDecadent yet wholesomeQuick + easy to make& SO delicious!

These are the perfect little treat to make during the fall and winter months. They’ve got you covered whether you want something on hand to satisfy sweet cravings during the work week or need a quick healthier dessert to bring to a gathering.

#9401. What Narcissists, Psychopaths And Sadists Have In Common

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Narcissists, psychopaths, sadists and manipulative people share a dark personality core that predicts selfish and antisocial choices.

This common tendency helps explain whether people exploit others, retaliate against them or refuse to trust them.

The crucial feature is a willingness to pursue personal interests at other people’s expense, accompanied by beliefs that justify doing so.

Known as the dark factor of personality, or D, this tendency brings together traits that can look quite different on the surface.

Narcissism involves an inflated sense of self-importance, Machiavellianism centres on manipulation, psychopathy includes callousness, and sadism involves enjoying others’ suffering.

The idea that these traits share an underlying disposition was established in earlier research examining their overlap and links to harmful behaviour (Moshagen et al., 2018).

The latest findings suggest that this shared core is more consistently associated with antisocial decisions than any of the four traits considered separately.

In other words, knowing what these personalities have in common may reveal more about their choices than knowing which particular label fits them.

The research involved over 10,000 people across ten studies using eight types of decision-making game.

Participants completed personality questionnaires before making hypothetical choices involving another person they did not know.

Depending on the game, they could decide how much money to share, whether to return someone’s trust, whether to retaliate or whether to cooperate.

Some situations allowed people to benefit themselves at someone else’s expense, while others explored whether they would trust another person when cooperation could benefit both.

People scoring higher on the dark factor consistently made fewer prosocial choices across all eight games.

The individual dark traits also generally predicted less prosocial behaviour, but their associations were weaker.

Once their shared dark core was taken into account, the separate traits usually added little to the explanation.

There were a few exceptions, particularly involving Machiavellianism in situations where distrust could influence decisions.

One possible explanation is that dark personality traits combine harmful tendencies with other characteristics that are not inherently antisocial.

For example, boldness does not necessarily involve harming anyone, while wanting admiration does not automatically mean exploiting others.

Earlier research proposed that these additional characteristics help distinguish dark traits from one another, while their shared core captures what makes them socially harmful (Bader et al., 2023).

Measuring a broad trait such as psychopathy may therefore mix callous self-interest with features that have little relevance to a particular moral decision.

Focusing on the common core could provide a clearer picture of someone’s willingness to disregard other people’s welfare.

Importantly, the dark factor extends beyond wanting a larger share of the rewards.

It also encompasses a readiness to hurt others and beliefs that can make selfish conduct seem acceptable.

Distrust may fit this pattern because expecting other people to behave selfishly can provide a convenient justification for doing the same.

That is a proposed psychological explanation, rather than evidence that distrust caused the choices observed here.

The findings do not mean that everyone with dark traits will behave selfishly in every situation.

Nor do they establish that personality caused the decisions participants made.

All the games were hypothetical, so participants were describing what they would choose rather than making decisions with real financial consequences.

This matters because associations between dark traits and antisocial choices can be stronger in hypothetical situations than when money is genuinely at stake.

Participants also volunteered through a website offering dark-personality assessments, so they were not a representative sample of the wider population.

Even with these qualifications, the results support a simpler account of apparently different dark personalities: much of their connection to harmful choices lies in the same underlying disregard for others.

The study was published in the journal Judgment and Decision Making (Hilbig & Thielmann, 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean
